newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bonds close higher in quiet trading.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bonds close higher in quiet trading.

text.p: Israeli bonds closed higher on Sunday in quiet trading with prices on CPI-linked long bonds falling on profit-taking, traders said.
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.13 pct to 107.11
Volume including Makams was 160 million shekels.
"Trading was mixed in CPI-linked bonds. Prices of long bonds fell slightly on profit-taking, while there was more demand for the medium-term bonds," said Ron Weisberg of IBI Investment House.
"The yield curve...is now moving to be a flat curve, which indicates that some players doubt there will be a further cut in interest rates," he said.
Weisberg said that after last week's interest rate cut yields on some of the CPI-linked long bonds had fallen below the four percent barrier.

"Trading in these bonds will now be stable with a negative trend in the coming weeks on profit-taking," he said, adding that by the end of summer he expected a new downward momentum because of low inflation and because in the long run the market expects a further cut in interest rates.

After the Israeli cabinet adopted a plan on Wednesday to widen the exchange rate band and adjust its diagonal rate, the central bank lowered its key lending rate 1.2 percentage points to an annualised 12.7 percent.

Some traders said they expected yields of the CPI-linked long bonds to remain at four percent. "We don't think yields will continue to fall because we don't expect a further cut in interest rates," said Eyal Segal of United Mizrahi Bank.
Prices of unlinked bonds continued to rise but at a slower rate due to the a low May CPI and the interest rate cut, Weisberg said.

Prices of dollar-linked bonds were higher after the skekel weakened against the dollar in Friday trading, Segal said. The representative rate was fixed on Friday at 3.4370 shekels to the dollar against 3.4190 shekels on Thursday.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with a maturity of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
- Shoshanna Solomon, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x233
